title: Indirect Statement
subtitle: The three patterns: ὅτι, accusative + infinitive, accusative + participle.
objectives: Understand the three constructions for indirect statement in Greek.
Use ὅτι + indicative to report statements.
Use accusative + infinitive with verbs of saying and thinking.
Use accusative + participle with verbs of knowing and perceiving.
Translate all three constructions into natural English.

sections.heading: Indirect statement
sections.body:
Indirect statement reports what someone said or thought without quoting their exact words. English uses 'that' clauses: 'He says that Socrates is wise.' Greek has three constructions:

1. ὅτι + indicative (like English 'that')
2. Accusative + infinitive (unique to Greek and Latin)
3. Accusative + participle (unique to Greek)

The choice of construction depends on the main verb. Some verbs prefer one construction; some allow multiple constructions.

sections.heading: ὅτι + indicative
sections.body:
λέγει ὅτι Σωκράτης σοφός ἐστιν.
'He says that Socrates is wise.'

ὅτι introduces a subordinate clause with the verb in the indicative. The tense of the verb in the ὅτι clause is the same as it would be in direct statement. This construction is closest to English and is common in Koine Greek (New Testament).

sections.heading: Accusative + infinitive
sections.body:
φησὶ Σωκράτη σοφὸν εἶναι.
'He says that Socrates is wise.'

The subject of the indirect statement is in the accusative (Σωκράτη). Any adjective or predicate noun agreeing with it is also in the accusative (σοφόν). The verb is an infinitive (εἶναι). This construction is common with verbs of saying and thinking (φημί, λέγω, νομίζω, οἴομαι).

Present infinitive = present time.
Aorist infinitive = past time.
Future infinitive = future time.

sections.heading: Accusative + participle
sections.body:
οἶδε Σωκράτη σοφὸν ὄντα.
'He knows that Socrates is wise.'

The subject of the indirect statement is in the accusative (Σωκράτη). The verb is a participle agreeing with the subject (ὄντα, accusative singular masculine of ὤν, the present participle of εἰμί). This construction is common with verbs of knowing and perceiving (οἶδα, γιγνώσκω, αἰσθάνομαι, ἀκούω, ὁράω).

Present participle = ongoing or contemporaneous action.
Aorist participle = completed or antecedent action.

sections.heading: From Plato
sections.body:
Plato, Apology 21b: λέγει ὅτι σοφώτατός ἐστι Σωκράτης.
'He says that Socrates is wisest.' (ὅτι + indicative)

Plato, Apology 21d: ἠγάσθην οἰόμενος αὐτὸν σοφὸν εἶναι.
'I marveled, thinking him to be wise.' (accusative + infinitive with οἴομαι)

items.prompt: What are the three constructions for indirect statement?
items.answer: ὅτι + indicative, accusative + infinitive, accusative + participle

items.prompt: Translate: λέγει ὅτι Σωκράτης σοφός ἐστιν.
items.answer: He says that Socrates is wise.
He says that Socrates is wise.
He knows that Socrates is wise.

sections.heading: Up next
sections.body: Lesson 4.8 introduces the perfect active. The perfect expresses the state resulting from completed action. λέλυκα means 'I have loosed' or 'I am in the state of having loosed'. The perfect uses reduplication and a new set of endings.

lesson_completion.criteria: Mark the lesson complete when you can recognize and translate all three constructions for indirect statement and can produce them correctly in Greek.
